content: 1. It is strongly recommended that tuberculosis (TB) patients who are also living with HIV should receive the same duration of daily TB treatment as those who are HIV-negative. This recommendation is supported by high-certainty evidence. 2. Individuals living with HIV who have both TB and histoplasmosis co-infections should receive TB therapy in accordance with the World Health Organization (WHO) treatment guidelines. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-certainty evidence. 3. In regions with a high burden of both HIV and TB, TB treatment can be provided to people living with HIV within HIV care settings, provided a TB diagnosis has been confirmed. This is a strong recommendation, although the evidence supporting it is of very low certainty. 4. Adults and adolescents living with HIV who are unlikely to have active TB should receive TB preventive treatment as part of their comprehensive HIV care. This includes individuals on antiretroviral therapy (ART), pregnant women, and those previously treated for TB, regardless of their level of immunosuppression or the availability of latent TB infection (LTBI) testing. This is a strong recommendation supported by high-certainty evidence. 5. Adults and adolescents living with HIV who are screened for TB using a clinical algorithm and report symptoms such as current cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats should be evaluated for TB and other diseases. If active TB is excluded, they should be offered preventive treatment. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 6. Chest radiography may be offered to people living with HIV who are on ART. Preventive treatment can be provided to those without abnormal radiographic findings. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-certainty evidence. 7. Testing for TB infection can be conducted using either the tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs). This is a strong recommendation, although the evidence is of very low certainty. 8. Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen-based skin tests (TBSTs) may also be used to test for TB infection. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-certainty evidence. 9. For the treatment of latent TB infection (LTBI), the following regimens are recommended regardless of HIV status: six or nine months of daily isoniazid, a three-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or a three-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. These are strong recommendations supported by moderate to high-certainty evidence. Additionally, a one-month regimen of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid or four months of daily rifampicin alone may be offered as alternatives. These are conditional recommendations with low to moderate-certainty evidence. 10. In settings with high TB transmission, adults and adolescents living with HIV who have an unknown or positive LTBI test and are unlikely to have active TB disease should receive at least 36 months of daily isoniazid preventive treatment (IPT). This should be provided regardless of ART status, degree of immunosuppression, history of previous TB treatment, or pregnancy. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-certainty evidence. 11. HIV testing services should be offered to all individuals with presumptive or diagnosed TB. This is a strong recommendation, although the evidence is of low quality. 12. All household contacts of individuals with HIV-associated TB should be offered HIV testing services. This is a strong recommendation supported by very low-quality evidence. 13. In settings with a high burden of HIV, all household and close contacts of people with TB should be offered HIV testing services. This is a strong recommendation with very low-quality evidence. 14. In settings with a low burden of HIV, household members and close contacts of people with TB who exhibit symptoms consistent with TB disease may be offered HIV testing services as part of their clinical evaluation. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 15. Partner services should be offered to individuals with HIV-associated TB. This is a strong recommendation supported by moderate-quality evidence. 16. A comprehensive package of interventions, including screening, treatment, and/or prophylaxis for major opportunistic infections, rapid ART initiation, and intensified adherence support, should be offered to all individuals presenting with advanced HIV disease. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. 17. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is recommended for all patients with HIV and drug-resistant TB who require second-line anti-TB drugs. ART should be initiated as early as possible, ideally within the first eight weeks of starting anti-TB treatment, regardless of CD4 cell count. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-certainty evidence. 18. Routine co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should be provided to all people living with HIV who have active TB disease, regardless of their CD4 cell count. This is a strong recommendation supported by high-certainty evidence. 19. In settings with a high burden of HIV and TB, ART should be initiated in TB treatment settings, with appropriate linkage to ongoing HIV care and ART services. This is a strong recommendation, although the evidence is of very low certainty. 20. People living with HIV are approximately 14 times more likely to develop TB disease compared to the general population. They also experience poorer TB treatment outcomes and have more than double the mortality rate during TB treatment compared to all individuals diagnosed with TB. 21. The WHO End TB Strategy, endorsed by the World Health Assembly in 2014, emphasizes integrated, patient-centered care and prevention of HIV-associated TB as key components. This strategy aims to achieve TB targets within the framework of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, including universal health coverage for all individuals affected by TB. 22. Despite significant progress in collaborative TB/HIV activities and advancements in TB prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, TB remains the leading cause of death among people living with HIV globally. In 2022, TB accounted for 27% of all HIV-related deaths worldwide. 23. WHO has updated its recommendations on screening, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of HIV-associated TB based on new scientific evidence. These updates include the benefits of early ART and TB preventive therapy (TPT), shorter rifamycin-based TPT regimens, and advancements in diagnostic tools such as C-reactive protein (CRP), chest X-rays, and molecular rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs). 24. WHO emphasizes the importance of systematic TB screening for people living with HIV at every health facility visit. This includes the use of the WHO-recommended four-symptom screen (W4SS), CRP, chest X-rays (with or without computer-aided detection), and mWRDs. 25. Collaborative TB/HIV activities have significantly reduced TB-related deaths among people living with HIV. However, gaps remain in the diagnosis and treatment of TB among this population, with only 64% of new TB cases among people with HIV being diagnosed and notified in 2022.
